newsitem.title: CHINA: China firms seen listing in London before Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: China firms seen listing in London before Tokyo.

text.p: Listing by Chinese companies on the Tokyo market next year is unlikely because of opposition from Japan's finance ministry, but listing in London is probable, brokers and diplomats said on Thursday.

A Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to allow for the listing of Chinese companies is due to be signed soon between the China Securities Regulatory Commission and the London Stock Exchange, said a British diplomat in Shanghai.
A Chinese investment banker said that Beijing would sign the MOU with London within the next two months, allowing for a first Chinese listing in London in 1997.
"The difference is that in London the financial industry and the government support a listing, while in Japan the securities firms are keen but the government is not," he said.
"The front-runners for a London listing are Jiangxi Copper Corporation and Shanghai Power," he said.
The commission is further away from signing a similar agreement with Tokyo, brokers said.
"I predict the chance of the agreement (with Tokyo) being signed this year as only 50-50," said one Japanese broker.
"The four big security brokers are very keen, but the ministry of finance is cautious because it thinks Chinese state companies cannot meet the requirements for a listing," he said.
"It needs a decision by politicians to accelerate the process and over-rule the bureaucrats," he added.

A second Japanese broker said that finance ministry officials did not want the agreement to be signed. "They are even more conservative than Chinese bureaucrats. They think that Chinese companies are not well enough run."

"There is also a debate with the Chinese government," he said. "Should China approve for Tokyo its best companies, which (the) Japanese would like to buy, or a less well-known company that needs money?"

The first broker said that in 1994, Japanese investors were keen on Chinese firms but their interest dropped after seeing the performance of Chinese H shares (mainland companies listed in Hong Kong) and with a revival of the Tokyo market.
"One or two years ago the Tokyo market needed new companies, but less so now," he said.

Brokers said that Japanese brokerages were courting for possible listing North China Pharmaceutical Ltd, the country's top colour television maker Sichuan Chang Hong Electronics, Shanghai Power and a Tianjin auto maker that produces Charade cars in co-operation with Daihatsu.

An official of Nomura's Shanghai office declined to say which companies they were talking to. "We hope there will be a listing next year but I do not know when the MOU will be signed." He declined further comment.
But brokers said Hong Kong would remain the main outside market for Chinese listings.

"Chinese firms prefer Hong Kong because they feel its investors understand them better, it is closer and they speak the same language. They feel investors in Europe and North America do not understand them well," the investment banker said.
More than 20 Chinese firms have listed H shares in Hong Kong and two have listed in New York.
